text: Indonesian painting has a long tradition and history in Indonesian art, with some of the world’s oldest paintings found in Indonesia due to the preservation of early works in cave environments. The earliest Indonesian paintings are prehistoric rock art, such as petroglyphs in the Maros caves in Sulawesi, which are approximately 40,000 years old and among the oldest known paintings globally. In November 2018, scientists discovered a figurative painting of an unknown animal in Lubang Jeriji Saléh on Borneo (Kalimantan), dated to over 40,000 years, possibly as old as 52,000 years. In December 2019, figurative cave paintings depicting pig hunting in the Maros-Pangkep karst in Sulawesi were estimated to be at least 43,900 years old, recognized as “the oldest pictorial record of storytelling and the earliest figurative artwork in the world.” In 2021, a pig-related cave painting in Indonesia was dated to over 45,500 years. These prehistoric paintings were created on cave walls and rocks, using techniques such as the aerograph—where hands were placed on walls and sprayed with chewing leaves or colored mineral stones—and clay with natural dyes from minerals and animal fats. The themes were often magical, and examples can be seen in Leang Pattakere Cave in South Sulawesi, depicting hunting scenes, and on the south coast of West Papua, showing ancestors. Hand silhouettes are common across many sites, including Seram Island, Berau Gulf, Arguni, and Kai Island, alongside motifs like human figures, boats, sun, moon, birds, fish, turtles, lizards, legs, and hog deer. After the prehistoric period, Indonesian culture developed expertise in stone construction, metal casting, agriculture, tools, sculpture, and batik, influenced by Hinduism from around the 5th century AD, leading to the emergence of writing. Art themes during this era included religion, mythology, legends, and historical stories, such as the Ramayana and Mahabharata in Balinese paintings. The Majapahit era used a wayang style with stylized, horizontal compositions, reflecting similarities between wayang kulit and Balinese paintings. Paintings used natural pigments from bark, leaves, soil, and soot, were made on elongated fabric without frames, resembling scroll paintings, and served as educational tools in temples and lontar manuscripts. In Bali, Hindu culture faced Islamic influence, leading to unique hybrid paintings recognized internationally. This development is divided into three phases: Kamasan, Pita Maha, and Young Artists painting. Islamic art in Indonesia centers in the Kraton, where artists combine knowledge of science, philosophy, and other arts. Depictions of living beings are avoided; instead, stylized animal and human motifs combined with Arabic script are used in mosque decorations and crafts. Paintings often depict stories from wayang or candra sangkala and prophet history, with some originating as glass paintings from Cirebon. Modern Indonesian painting began with Dutch colonialism, influenced by European romanticism, and was shaped by figures like Raden Saleh Syarif Bustaman (1807–1880), who studied under A.A.J. Payen and later in Europe with Cornellius Krusemen and Andreas Schefhout, becoming the first Indonesian to study fine arts abroad and a respected court painter. Raden Saleh is considered a pioneer, though Indonesian painting did not follow the European Renaissance stages. After the revolution, painters shifted from romantic themes to "populist" themes, rejecting natural beauty as a symbol of capitalist enemies in the communist ideology. Limited access to paints and canvases led to simpler, abstract forms. The Cultural Manifesto Movement in the 1950s encouraged artists to free their work from political propaganda, leading to expressionism. Modernism later introduced alternative art forms like installation and performance art, which emerged widely in art colleges between 1993 and 1996, followed by "collaboration" as a trend in 1996–1997. Conventional painting became more of an investment than community appreciation. Modern Indonesian art is deeply connected to European traditions, influenced by post-impressionism (early 18th century), which emphasized individualism and experimentation in materials, techniques, and expression. This contact began through European painters visiting Indonesia, inspiring new artistic directions. In the mid-19th century, Indonesian artists primarily used traditional regional styles with decorative potential, such as in Bali, Java, Toraja, and Kalimantan. S. Sudjojono (1913–1986) led a group of painters who never studied in Europe, including Agus Djaya Suminta, L. Sutioso, Rameli, Abdul Salam, Otto Jaya, S. Sudiarjo, Emiria Sunassa, Saptarita Latif, Herbert Hutagalung, S. Tutur, Hendro Jasmara, and Sutioso. In 1938, they formed the Association of Indonesian Drawing Experts (PERSAGI) in Jakarta to promote an authentic Indonesian style through sketches of local life. After returning from Europe, Abdullah S.R. (1878–1941) developed the Indonesia Jelita (Mooi Indie) style in Bandung, emphasizing the beauty and peaceful nature of Indonesia, often portraying romantic and serene natural scenes for foreign tourists. Before this, Dutch colonial authorities employed foreign painters such as W. G. Hofker (Netherlands), R. Locatelli (Italy), Le Mayeur (Netherlands), Roland Strasser (Switzerland), E. Dezentje (Netherlands), and Rudolf Bonnet (Netherlands). During the Japanese occupation in 1942, PERSAGI was disbanded, but grassroots artists emerged. In 1945, Japan established Japan Keimin Bunka Shidoso (Cultural Center) with former PERSAGI members like Agus Djaya Suminta and S. Sudjojono as teachers, supporting artistic activities. Despite economic hardship, artistic life flourished, with exhibitions held by painters such as Basuki Abdullah, Affandi, Kartono Yudhokusumo, Nyoman Ngedon, Hendra Gunawan, Henk Nantung, and Otto Jaya to promote national identity. Post-independence, painting became a medium of national struggle, evident in struggle posters and battle sketches, notably by Djajengasmoro and his Front Painter group. In 1946, after the government moved to Yogyakarta, painters relocated there, forming the Community Arts Association in 1946, later joining the Young Indonesian Artists (SIM) group in 1947, founded in Madiun by Sudjojono. In 1949, R. J. Katamsi and other SIM members, along with People's Painters, POETRA, and Budayan Taman Siswa, established the Indonesian Fine Arts Academy (ASRI), now known as ISI, to train aspiring artists. Key figures included S. Soedjojono, Hendra Gunawan, Djajengasmoro, Kusnadi, and Sindusiswono. In Bandung, the Center for the Higher Education for Teachers of Pictures, led by Syafe'i Soemardja and assisted by Mochtar Apin, Ahmad Sadali, Sudjoko, and Edi Karta Subarna, became the Fine Arts Department at ITB in 1959. In 1964, the Department of Fine Arts Education at IKIP Bandung (now Indonesian Education University) was founded by Barli, Karmas, Popo Iskandar, Radiosuto, and Wiyoso Yudoseputo, with alumni including Oho Garha, Nana Banna, Hidayat, Dadang MA, and Hardiman. Fine arts departments later spread to other IKIPs across Indonesia. Around 1974, young artists emerged in various regions, including Jim Supangkat, Syahrinur Prinka, Satyagraha, F.X. Harsono, Dede Eri Supria, and Munni Ardi. Their first exhibition was at Taman Ismail Marzuki in Jakarta. These young artists challenged traditional definitions of art, rejected academic elitism, questioned established boundaries, avoided framing, used diverse media and concepts, and created works inspired by sacred elements.
